name: Docker
tagline: Container tooling to package applications and make development and deployment environments more reproducible.
description: Docker packages applications into containers for repeatable environments; current plan details and independent ratings are not verified here.
pros: Container images can make dependencies and runtime assumptions more reproducible.
A consistent image can support local development, CI and deployment workflows.
Image scanning and versioned releases can be included in a documented delivery process.
A clean build can test reproducibility across developer and CI environments.
Image scanning and rollback can be included in the release checklist.
cons: Containers do not by themselves provide production orchestration, monitoring or recovery.
Images require ongoing patching, secret hygiene and supply-chain review.
Networking, persistent storage and runtime differences must be tested in the target environment.

content.title: Build a reproducible image
content.body: Create a minimal image for a representative service and document base image, dependency versions, build context and runtime user. Build it from a clean environment and confirm that the same artifact is used for testing and deployment. Avoid embedding credentials or environment-specific secrets in the image.

content.title: Security and supply chain
content.body: Scan dependencies and image layers, keep base images updated and define who owns critical vulnerabilities. Use least privilege, a non-root runtime where feasible and a documented image provenance process. Treat an image scan as one control, not proof that the application is secure.

content.title: Local development and CI
content.body: Test that a new teammate can start the application, run tests and reproduce a known failure using the documented setup. Confirm how volumes, ports, environment variables and test services behave in CI. Keep local convenience settings separate from production configuration.

content.title: Production runtime
content.body: Determine whether the workload needs a single container, a managed container service or orchestration. Test health checks, graceful shutdown, logs, scaling, persistent data and rollback. Docker alone does not decide how production scheduling, networking or recovery will work.

content.title: Operations and cost
content.body: Estimate registry storage, compute, logging, networking, orchestration and engineering time. Document image update cadence, release tags, rollback and incident ownership. Validate the full deployment path in the target platform before moving a production service.

content.title: Pilot acceptance criteria
content.body: A developer should be able to build and run the same version from a clean checkout using documented commands. Test the image in CI and in the target runtime, and confirm configuration is injected securely at runtime. Record build reproducibility, startup behavior and how quickly a patched image can be released.

content.title: Failure cases and recovery
content.body: Test a missing environment variable, an unavailable dependency, an image with a known vulnerable package and a failed health check. Verify the service fails safely, logs are useful and rollback restores the prior image. Document who owns base-image updates and how exceptions expire.

content.title: Decision record
content.body: Document image ownership, base image policy, registry access, scan gates, runtime privileges, persistent data, deployment platform and recovery process. Compare the ongoing operations effort with a managed runtime where appropriate. Containerization is a packaging choice, not a complete production architecture.

faqs.question: Who should evaluate Docker?
faqs.answer: Evaluate Docker when its primary workflow matches a documented requirement. Test a representative task and verify current capabilities and limits directly with the vendor.

faqs.question: How should a team test Docker?
faqs.answer: Use the same real input, expected outcome and acceptance criteria each time. Record pass, partial pass, fail or unknown, including setup time, manual work and failure handling.

faqs.question: Which limitations should be checked in Docker?
faqs.answer: Check the exact plan, integrations, permissions, export, data retention, recovery and ongoing administration. Treat untested or undocumented capabilities as unknown until confirmed.

faqs.question: Are Docker prices and ratings independently verified here?
faqs.answer: No. Current prices, plan limits and independent ratings are not verified in this review. Check official documentation and obtain a dated quote before purchase.

faqs.question: What should be confirmed before adopting Docker?
faqs.answer: Confirm the core workflow, access controls, integrations, data export, account offboarding, support responsibilities and renewal terms. Assign an owner for the implementation and ongoing review.

aiFeatures: Docker AI assistant for Dockerfile optimization

learningCurve: Steep — requires dedicated training time for full proficiency
whoShouldUse: Docker is ideal for small to mid-size teams that need a reliable developer tools solution without excessive complexity. It works well for organizations with 5-200 users who prioritize ease of use and quick deployment.
whoShouldNotUse: Docker may be overwhelming for users who only need basic developer tools functionality. Its extensive feature set can create unnecessary complexity for simple use cases.
